title: AWS OIDC flow
subtitle: Azure DevOps to AWS with no stored secret. Everything you need to audit ACN-2026-31070 and then any AWS authentication case.

create.t: AWS: Create an OIDC identity provider

blog.t: AWS blog: Federate into AWS from Azure DevOps

ct.t: AWS: Logging IAM and STS calls with CloudTrail

keys.t: AWS: IAM and STS condition keys

controls.A1: Provider is configured with the org-specific Azure DevOps issuer URL. No generic, test, personal or non-ADO orgs.
controls.A2: Provider and every role trust policy check the audience api://AzureADTokenExchange with StringEquals. No wildcards.
controls.A3: Federated trust allows only sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity for the Azure DevOps provider. Nothing broader.
controls.A4: Each role trust restricts the sub claim to the approved service connection, WBG format, no wildcards.
controls.A5: Each role has only the actions and resource ARNs its pipelines need (least privilege).
controls.A6: Production role is not assumable by dev, test or unrelated service connections. Separate roles and subs.
controls.P1: Only an approved admin path can change the provider, trust policies, permissions and session settings. Pipeline roles cannot edit themselves.
controls.S1: Old access keys are removed and revoked. No static-key fallback anywhere (service connections, variable groups, YAML, scripts, repos, agents).
controls.S2: OIDC tokens and STS temporary credentials never appear in logs, traces, artifacts, outputs, caches or error messages.
controls.C1: Inventory of the provider ARN and all roles that trust it. Remove obsolete ones.
controls.D1: Change control and independent review for role ARN, service connection, OIDC enablement, duration and auth scripts.
controls.D2: Pre-production test shows success for the right connection and denial for wrong audience, wrong subject, unauthorised connection, removed trust.
controls.L1: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is logged for every in-scope role, success and failure, with enough context to match a pipeline run.
controls.L2: Create, change and delete of the provider, roles, trust policies and permission policies are logged.
controls.M1: Alerts for repeated failures, unapproved sub or aud, unexpected assumptions, unauthorised changes.
controls.R1: Documented and tested way to disable a compromised federation and revoke leftover keys.

tree.s: A pipeline proves who it is with a signed token, and AWS swaps that token for short-lived credentials. No key is stored anywhere.

k.s: Who can talk to AWS, and with what proof. The base layer under everything else.
The container that holds your AWS resources and identities. Every role ARN carries a 12 digit account ID (the case uses 706569143085).
k.w: You must read ARNs fast: arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:role/NAME. Wrong account in a trust policy is a finding.

k.s: An IAM user holds long-term credentials: an access key ID and a secret access key. They stay valid until deleted. Whoever copies them becomes that user.
k.w: This is what the project removes. You audit that none remain.

k.s: An identity with permissions but no password and no keys. Anyone allowed to assume it borrows it for a session.
k.w: The whole design is a role that the pipeline assumes. Two policies sit on it: trust and permission.

k.s: STS (Security Token Service) hands out temporary credentials: access key ID, secret key, session token. They expire (default 1 hour for web identity, 15 minutes to the role maximum of 1 to 12 hours).
k.w: Explains why a leaked pipeline credential is far less dangerous, and what duration setting to review.

k.s: AWS recommends workloads use temporary credentials from roles, and keep long-term keys only where nothing else works.
k.w: The justification you quote when writing a finding about a stored key.

k.s: The language the pipeline and AWS use to trust each other.
A system that vouches for identities. Here: Azure DevOps vouches for a pipeline's service connection.
k.w: You need to know which IdP a provider in AWS points at, and who runs it.

k.s: OpenID Connect: a standard way for an IdP to prove identity to another system by issuing a signed token.
k.w: Names the protocol in the audit documents. Not something you configure, something you recognise.

k.s: A JSON Web Token is the signed token. It carries claims: named facts such as who issued it, who it is for, who it is about.
k.w: Every trust-policy condition is a test on a claim.

k.s: iss = issuer URL (https://vstoken.dev.azure.com/{OrgGUID}). aud = intended recipient (api://AzureADTokenExchange, fixed for Azure DevOps). sub = subject (sc://{Org}/{Project}/{ServiceConnection}).
k.w: These three strings are the lock. Five of the sixteen controls test them.

k.s: The IdP publishes /.well-known/openid-configuration and a jwks_uri with public keys. AWS uses them to verify the token signature.
k.w: Explains how AWS trusts a token without a shared secret. Useful when a provider fails to create.

k.s: IAM accepts a token up to five minutes after its exp time to allow for clock skew.
k.w: Context for replay and timing questions.

k.s: Four steps from pipeline to AWS resource. Learn this picture and the rest hangs off it.
A saved, authenticated link from Azure Pipelines to an outside service. For AWS it stores the role ARN and the use OIDC option, and no keys.
k.w: Its name is inside sub. Whoever can use or edit it controls who reaches AWS.

k.s: Azure DevOps mints the OIDC token for the running pipeline. The AWS toolkit logs it as 'OIDC Token generated'.
k.w: The log line is the easiest place to read the real iss, aud and sub.

k.s: The STS call that swaps the token plus a role ARN for temporary credentials. It needs no AWS credentials to make.
k.w: This exact name appears in trust policies (A3) and in CloudTrail (L1).

k.s: Evidence lines: 'Getting OIDC Token', 'Assuming role via OIDC Token', an assumed-role ARN, 'aws sts get-caller-identity', a successful 'aws s3 ls'.
k.w: Your case's captured evidence is this. Know what it proves and what it cannot prove.

k.s: arn:aws:sts::ACCOUNT:assumed-role/ROLE/SESSION means a role is in use, not a user. SESSION is aws-vsts-tools by default.
k.w: One glance tells you whether a static user key could have been used.

k.s: The first lock: AWS is told which issuer to believe.
Must be https and match the token's iss. For Azure DevOps it ends with that organisation's GUID.
k.w: A provider for any other org, test org or personal org is a finding.

k.s: api://AzureADTokenExchange is the audience registered on the provider.
k.w: Must be exact and must also be checked again in each role.

k.s: List the provider ARNs and which roles trust each. Remove obsolete ones when the org or connection is retired.
k.w: Control C1. Stale trust is quiet risk.

k.s: The template mentions a thumbprint. This map has not opened the source on it, so treat it as unverified.
k.w: Ask the architect whether this check still applies before you test it.

k.s: The second lock, and the heart of the audit: exactly who may become this role.
Trust policy says who may assume the role. Permission policy says what the role may do. Different documents, different questions.
k.w: Mixing these up is the most common reviewer mistake.

k.s: Names the one OIDC provider ARN allowed to vouch.
k.w: Should list only the Azure DevOps provider, no other principals.

k.s: Only sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Anything broader widens who can get in.
k.w: Control A3 in one line.

k.t: Condition keys carry the provider URL
k.s: Keys look like vstoken.dev.azure.com/{OrgGUID}:aud and :sub. The prefix tells AWS which provider's claim to test.
k.w: Explains why the key names differ per provider and why a wrong prefix silently never matches.

k.s: StringEquals is exact. The Like operators accept wildcards, so StringLike on sub with sc://Org/* lets every service connection in the org in.
k.w: The classic fail. Learn to spot a * in aud or sub in seconds.

k.s: If a condition key is absent from the request, the match is false. For NotLike style operators it is true instead.
k.w: Why one operator choice can fail open.

k.s: Production uses its own role with its own sub. A dev or test connection must not match it.
k.w: Control A6. Compare the sub of the prod role with the dev connection names.

k.s: What the pipeline can do once it is in.
Effect, Action, Resource, Condition. Read any AWS policy by finding these four.
k.w: You will read many policies. This is the grammar.

k.s: List only the actions and resource ARNs the pipeline needs. A * on Action or Resource is the red flag.
k.w: Control A5. Compare the policy to what the pipeline actually does.

k.s: A request is allowed only if a policy allows it, and an explicit deny always wins.
k.w: Authentication passing but AccessDenied appearing is this step, not a trust problem.

k.s: Extra layers that can only narrow what a role may do. Allowed means allowed by all of them.
k.w: Why a policy that looks wide may still be harmless, or may be blocked by something you did not read.

k.s: The right to change the provider, trust policies and permissions must sit with an approved admin path, not with the pipeline role itself.
k.w: Control P1. A role that can edit its own trust policy can widen its own access.

k.s: An AWS tool that can generate least-privilege policies from real activity and validate policies.
k.w: A practical way to back an A5 finding with data.

k.s: Where the old keys hide and where new secrets can leak.
Switch the service connection to OIDC, then delete the stored keys and revoke them in AWS. No fallback copy left in variable groups, YAML, scripts, repos or agents.
k.w: Control S1. Check both sides: the IAM user key status in AWS and the Azure DevOps places.

k.s: Tokens and temporary keys must not appear in logs, debug traces, artifacts, outputs, caches or error messages.
k.w: Control S2. Look at failure output and debug runs, not only the green run.

k.s: Changes to role ARN, service connection, OIDC enablement, duration and auth scripts need independent review.
k.w: Control D1. Ask for pull request or change record evidence.

k.s: The pipeline variable aws.rolecredential.maxduration sets how long credentials last, 900 to 43200 seconds.
k.w: Long duration widens the window if a credential leaks.

k.s: Before production, show success for the right connection and denial for wrong audience, wrong subject, an unauthorised connection and a removed trust.
k.w: Control D2. Success-only test records are a finding.

k.s: How you know who did what, and what happens when it goes wrong.
AWS service that records IAM and STS API calls. Event history shows recent events. A trail stores them long term in S3.
k.w: Your main AWS-side evidence source.

k.s: Every AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity call, success and failure, should be recorded with enough context to link it to a pipeline run.
k.w: Control L1. Ask for a sample event and check what identity fields it holds.

k.s: Create, modify and delete of the provider, roles, trust policies and permission policies must be logged.
k.w: Control L2.

k.s: Alerts for repeated failures, unapproved sub or aud, unexpected assumptions, and unauthorised changes.
k.w: Control M1. Ask to see the rule, not just a statement.

k.s: A tested way to cut off federation: narrow or remove the sub trust, disable the service connection, or disable the role. Then review STS events and revoke leftover keys.
k.w: Control R1. Written but never exercised is a finding.

k.s: The skill that turns knowledge into findings.
For each control: what does it protect, where is the evidence, what does pass look like, what is the finding if it fails.
k.w: The loop you will repeat sixteen times.

k.s: A pipeline log shows the pipeline's view only. Trust policy, role permissions and CloudTrail must be opened in AWS. A statement is not evidence.
k.w: Stops you passing a control on a screenshot that cannot prove it.

k.s: The final advisory lists 16 controls. The solution architect template adds 14 validation checks. You were told 20+.
k.w: Confirm the list with the requester before you start.

k.s: Check 5 names AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE, not seen in the Azure DevOps evidence. Check 3 allows only s3:ListBucket, but the evidence ran 'aws s3 ls'. Check 1 mentions a thumbprint. Unverified here.
k.w: Questions for the architect, not conclusions.

k.s: Control, what you saw, where you saw it, why it matters, what fixes it.
k.w: The deliverable.

k.s: The same parts in other clothes. This is what makes the base reusable on harder cases.
Human users should reach AWS through an identity provider and temporary credentials. AWS recommends IAM Identity Center for central access.
k.w: The human-user version of the same idea.

k.s: Same trust idea with a different token format and different condition keys.
k.w: You will see it on workforce cases.

k.s: A broker for sign-up and sign-in of app users, usable with OIDC.
k.w: App-user cases rather than pipeline cases.

k.s: Same pattern: a different issuer, different sub format, same two locks and same permission policy.
k.w: Transfers straight from this case.

k.s: A role assumed from another account or by an AWS service. Service-linked roles are owned by the service.
k.w: Appears whenever one account reaches into another.

k.t: Five questions for any new case
k.s: Who is the IdP? What proves the caller? What restricts which caller? What can it do after? Where is it logged?
k.w: The transferable checklist.

ui.learner: I am a security auditor. I know basic computing and nothing about AWS.
